title: Depression, Low Mood & Motivation
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

glossary.definition: A common response to loss or disappointment that can vary through the day.
glossary.example: Someone feels down after being rejected for a job they wanted.
glossary.limit: A short spell of sadness does not, on its own, establish a depressive disorder.

glossary.definition: Doing less or having less contact with activities and people than before.
glossary.example: A student repeatedly cancels enjoyable plans after a setback.
glossary.limit: Taking some time alone may be helpful; the effect of withdrawal depends on what it changes.

glossary.definition: Finding less enjoyment in activities that previously felt rewarding.
glossary.example: A person no longer enjoys meeting friends, even when they attend.
glossary.limit: Loss of pleasure is one possible symptom; it needs to be understood alongside duration and other changes.

glossary.definition: A broader pattern of symptoms and impairment assessed over time, rather than a synonym for feeling sad.

nodes.title: What sadness means
nodes.body:
A common response to loss or disappointment that can vary through the day.

For example: Someone feels down after being rejected for a job they wanted.

One important limit: A short spell of sadness does not, on its own, establish a depressive disorder.

nodes.title: Find the first concept

nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

lessons.title: First notice what happened
lessons.teach: Read what is said before deciding why anyone said it.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Callum has felt sad and unmotivated since failing to get a job he hoped would change his situation. Jules calls to check in.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.
nodes.scenario: Callum has felt sad and unmotivated since failing to get a job he hoped would change his situation. Jules calls to check in.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I didn't get it. I've been miserable all week.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: That mattered to you. What has the week been like?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I've cancelled plans because I don't feel like talking.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Have there been moments when anything felt enjoyable?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.
checks.counterexample: A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

items.label: “I didn't get it. I've been miserable all week.”
Sadness following disappointment is understandable. Withdrawal can reduce immediate social demands but also reduce access to rewarding experiences, which may maintain low mood.
“That mattered to you. What has the week been like?”
Callum may need time to grieve a meaningful loss; a short period of retreat is not automatically a maladaptive cycle.

nodes.body:

lessons.title: Two explanations can sound reasonable
lessons.teach: Evidence should be able to change which explanation you prefer.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Sadness following disappointment is understandable. Withdrawal can reduce immediate social demands but also reduce access to rewarding experiences, which may maintain low mood.

Another possibility: Callum may need time to grieve a meaningful loss; a short period of retreat is not automatically a maladaptive cycle.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Examine duration, pervasiveness, associated symptoms and functional change while considering bereavement, stress and physical health. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Examine duration, pervasiveness, associated symptoms and functional change while considering bereavement, stress and physical health.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: Over the next month Callum's low mood persists most days, his sleep changes markedly and he struggles to manage basic responsibilities.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The duration and broader functional changes make an assessment for depression more relevant than in the first week, though the vignette remains insufficient for diagnosis.
nodes.counterexample: A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.teach: You have the concepts. Now practise using them without jumping beyond the evidence.

modules.title: Sadness after disappointment
modules.bookTitle: What low mood is and isn't

lessons.title: When sadness follows a loss
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of sadness after disappointment.

nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
Sadness after disappointment is understandable, and time course matters when considering clinical depression. Withdrawal may offer shelter from reminders but also reduce opportunities for comfort and reward. The task is to notice what happens next without rushing from a two-day experience to a diagnosis.

A depressive episode can follow a clear trigger. Duration, severity, other symptoms and functional consequences all require consideration.
nodes.sources: NICE NG222, depression in adults; behavioural activation models.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: NICE NG222, depression in adults; behavioural activation models.
nodes.scenario: Mara was rejected for a job she cared deeply about two days ago.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I don't feel like seeing anyone after that email.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: You put months into that application. What's hardest right now?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I keep thinking I'll never get anywhere.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Has the feeling changed at all these past two days?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: A little when I saw my sister, then it came back when I read the email.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: We can take it seriously without deciding yet what kind of longer-term pattern this is.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Mara may prefer temporary solitude after disappointment without any unhelpful process.
Mara may be interpreting one painful rejection as evidence of a permanently unsuccessful future.
Mara may be entering a depressive episode that needs further assessment.
A previous disagreement may have shaped the response, making the present conversation part of a longer pattern.
options.feedback: History could matter, but that earlier pattern has not yet been established.

options.label: Callum may be grieving a meaningful opportunity and need time to adjust rather than immediate clinical intervention.
options.feedback: The timing of the rejection supports this, although prolonged functional impairment changes the assessment.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Mara may be interpreting one painful rejection as evidence of a permanently unsuccessful future. Mara may be entering a depressive episode that needs further assessment. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: A depressive episode can follow a clear trigger. Duration, severity, other symptoms and functional consequences all require consideration.

checks.prompt: You are Mara. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

options.label: A previous disagreement may have shaped the response, making the present conversation part of a longer pattern.
options.reply: We can take it seriously without deciding yet what kind of longer-term pattern this is.
options.consequence: Backing away can ease pressure now while leaving the original concern unresolved.
options.feedback: History could matter, but that earlier pattern has not yet been established.

options.label: Before making any decision, I'd like you to explain exactly why you responded that way.
options.reply: Has the feeling changed at all these past two days?
options.consequence: Demanding a definitive motive may provoke another defence rather than settle the issue.

options.label: Let's ask someone else to intervene before discussing this further.
options.reply: Does it make the sadness easier?

nodes.explanation: A sound response is judged by what it makes possible, not by whether it can instantly change somebody else. Choose one manageable activity linked to something you value, and monitor whether participation changes your experience rather than waiting for motivation.
nodes.counterexample: A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

nodes.title: If the first response fails
nodes.prompt: The other person rejects a reasonable direct request and the practical concern is unresolved. What next?
nodes.explanation: Escalation can be proportionate when a direct attempt has failed. Its safety and usefulness depend on the situation. A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.

options.label: Repeat reassurance until the other person no longer experiences the issue as threatening.
options.feedback: Reassurance can help but cannot guarantee action on a concrete problem.

options.label: Ignore the disappointment and keep your schedule exactly as before.
options.feedback: This makes the unresolved issue reviewable without needing to diagnose the other person.

nodes.title: Correct the inference
nodes.prompt: Someone says: “That tells us what sort of person they really are.” Which revision is most defensible?
nodes.explanation: A working interpretation can be informative without being a diagnosis. A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.

options.feedback: Possible explanations need not be equally supported. We should compare their fit with the actual evidence.

nodes.title: Which evidence matters most?
nodes.prompt: You want to distinguish the working hypothesis from its strongest alternative. Which investigation would provide the most discriminating information?
nodes.explanation: Investigate a difference that the rival explanations predict. Examine duration, pervasiveness, associated symptoms and functional change while considering bereavement, stress and physical health.
nodes.counterexample: A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

options.label: Ask both people to describe how strongly they felt during the conversation.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling matters, but it does not establish its cause.

options.label: Examine duration, pervasiveness, associated symptoms and functional change while considering bereavement, stress and physical health.
options.feedback: This gathers information that could strengthen or weaken the explanation, rather than merely confirming an impression.

options.label: Ask the person affected whether the behaviour seems consistent with their overall impression of the speaker.
options.feedback: Impact and perception matter for responding; they are less decisive about the other person’s hidden motives.

options.label: Find one more occasion when the characters disagreed, without checking what the circumstances were.
options.feedback: Another incident is useful only if we compare the circumstances and plausible explanations.

options.label: Ask both people what they expected would happen next and compare their predictions with the observed outcome.
options.feedback: Expectations matter, but retrospective reports may be incomplete or influenced by hindsight.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A student feels low after a breakup and gradually stops attending activities that previously provided enjoyment, even as the initial acute distress changes.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

nodes.title: Apply the method elsewhere
nodes.prompt: Consider this different situation: A student feels low after a breakup and gradually stops attending activities that previously provided enjoyment, even as the initial acute distress changes. What is the strongest next step?
nodes.explanation: Transfer the reasoning method rather than an explanation from the first case. A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.
nodes.counterexample: A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.

options.label: Treat the visible similarity as a reliable indication that the behaviour has the same psychological function.
options.feedback: Similar behaviours can protect very different interests depending on the context.

options.label: Consider what the person could be trying to gain or avoid, then test that explanation against the circumstances and credible alternatives.
options.feedback: This asks what the behaviour might accomplish and how we could check.

options.label: Postpone all interpretation until the person can give an account of their private motives.
options.feedback: A perfect self-report may be unavailable. Tentative, revisable inferences can still be useful.

options.label: Judge whether the behaviour is socially acceptable first, since that provides the best evidence about why it happened.
options.feedback: Judging the consequences of a behaviour is important, but consequences do not by themselves establish motive.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Sadness following disappointment is understandable. Withdrawal can reduce immediate social demands but also reduce access to rewarding experiences, which may maintain low mood.

A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

glossary.definition: A common response to loss or disappointment that can vary through the day.
glossary.example: Someone feels down after being rejected for a job they wanted.
glossary.limit: A short spell of sadness does not, on its own, establish a depressive disorder.

glossary.definition: Doing less or having less contact with activities and people than before.
glossary.example: A student repeatedly cancels enjoyable plans after a setback.
glossary.limit: Taking some time alone may be helpful; the effect of withdrawal depends on what it changes.

glossary.definition: Finding less enjoyment in activities that previously felt rewarding.
glossary.example: A person no longer enjoys meeting friends, even when they attend.
glossary.limit: Loss of pleasure is one possible symptom; it needs to be understood alongside duration and other changes.

glossary.definition: A broader pattern of symptoms and impairment assessed over time, rather than a synonym for feeling sad.
glossary.example: Low mood lasts for weeks and affects sleep, concentration and daily responsibilities.
glossary.limit: A story or online quiz cannot establish a diagnosis without proper assessment.
